about: Rule data for speakhuman_lint.py. Regexes use Python re syntax, compiled case-insensitive; (?-i:...) makes a span case-sensitive. A regex entry is a string or an object with re, scope (block|sentence), position (any|first|lead|last|last2|only; lead = the first sentence, or the second after a short opener such as 'Great question!'), contexts, and optional unless (skip a hit when its sentence matches), unless_prev (skip when one of the two sentences before it matches) and skip_roles (skip blocks whose HTML class or tag marks them as pullquote, summary, dialogue, nav or select). A rule may set skip_paths, a regex on the file path. kind: pattern | density | engine | manual (manual rules have no code; they exist for the human review checklist). Severity: error (high precision), warn (candidate), info (density and rhythm).

rules.name: Non-ASCII typography
rules.message: Non-ASCII typography: em or en dash, curly quote, ellipsis character, arrow, bullet, check mark, emoji or invisible space. These read as machine-written and often break in plain-text destinations.
rules.fix: Retype in plain ASCII. Replace a dash with a period, comma, colon or parentheses, and rewrite the sentence if it leaned on the dash. Straight quotes, three periods, and the word 'to' in place of an arrow.
rules.false_positive_note: Letters with diacritics (a cited surname such as Parra Escartin with its accent), math signs (multiplication, division, plus-minus, degree) and currency signs are not matched here, and any other non-ASCII character is reported by non-ascii-other as a warning. HTML entities for names and math (í, ×) are ignored. For quoted foreign text, add <!-- slop-ok: non-ascii-typography --> on the line.

rules.name: House-banned vocabulary
rules.message: Word on the house avoid list (stock AI vocabulary). Replace it with the plain word or cut the clause. Add words with extra_banned_words in your profile.
rules.fix: Use the plain word or say the specific thing: leverage -> use; seamless -> cut it; delve -> look at; foster -> build; empower -> let; pivotal -> say why it matters; landscape -> market or field; unlock -> open or allow; holistic -> whole, or list the parts; actionable -> say what to do.
rules.false_positive_note: Four of these words have a literal meaning, so they match only in their stock sense: leverage as a verb with an object (leverage our data), foster with an abstract object (foster a culture of trust), landscape after a market or industry word or as something to navigate (the competitive landscape), and unlock with an abstract object (unlock the full potential). Leverage on a balance sheet, foster care, a landscape that slopes toward a river and unlocking a card or a door are not flagged. A regulation quoted verbatim keeps its own wording; suppress that line.

rules.name: Strict X-not-Y forms
rules.message: The X-not-Y construction: a claim built on a negated foil ('It's not X, it's Y'; 'not just X, but Y'). State what the thing is and stop.
rules.fix: State Y and stop. 'The question isn't the model. It's the eval.' becomes 'The eval matters more than the model.' Keep a contrast only when it corrects a belief the reader actually holds, and then write it as a plain statement of what is true.
rules.false_positive_note: Human writers use this device too ('not because X, but because Y'), so it is a warning, and under the default density policy a single use is information. Keep a contrast that corrects a belief the reader actually holds. The engine also fires on 'The office is not in Texas. It is in Delaware.', which is the same device.

rules.name: Stapled-on ending
rules.message: The last paragraph of the piece carries no number and no name from the piece. Check that the ending is grounded.
rules.fix: Tie the ending to a specific number, person or fact already established, or cut it. Do not invent a new image to close on.
rules.false_positive_note: A closing line that calls back to the opening scene can work without a number; read it against the opening.

bad: In the end, every tool is only as good as the people who use it, and the best ones disappear into the work.

rules.name: Abandoned metaphor left in labels
rules.message: Labels and headings that only make sense under a frame the piece dropped.
rules.fix: When a frame is cut, list its words in <!-- slop-lint retired: ... --> and rename every hit (retired-vocabulary does the search).
rules.false_positive_note: A metaphor still carrying weight elsewhere in the piece can stay.

bad: Fuel for growth
Turning the flywheel
2 of 4 gears turning
Launchpad calculator

rules.name: Signature metaphor reused in consecutive pieces
rules.message: The central metaphor or signature device repeats the previous piece.
rules.fix: Check what the last one or two months of articles used (frontmatter dates) and pick something else. Declare the previous piece's signature words as retired so the engine catches them.
rules.false_positive_note: Reuse after one to two months is fine. Template chrome shared by every article is exempt.

bad: 'the flywheel' as the spine of the post right after the flywheel post

rules.name: Restatement presented as new information
rules.message: A rewrite repeats the same number or claim in new words (often with a citation added) and gives the reader nothing new to act on.
rules.fix: Keep only the version that tells the reader something new they can use; cut the rest.
rules.false_positive_note: Adding a missing source to an unsourced number is a real fix on its own.

bad: Each new hire costs $4,000 to onboard and $900 a year in software. (rewritten with the same $900 and three citations)

rules.name: Over-explained instructions
rules.message: Rationale and caveats before the steps.
rules.fix: A bare numbered list. The reader will ask if they need the why.
rules.false_positive_note: One line of context that picks which procedure applies is fine.

bad: (three paragraphs of background, then: step 1 do this, step 2 do this)
good: 1. Open the board. 2. Click it. 3. Pick Settings.

rules.name: Voice and frame mismatch
rules.message: A line attributes a framing or motive the author would not use about themselves or their work.
rules.fix: Use the author's own stated framing, or ask. Read the line as a skeptical buyer would and check what it implies.
rules.false_positive_note: Person-specific; apply only against the author's stated framing, which lives in the profile voice notes.

bad: what the sales sheet said the plan included
I have been the go-to fixer on every team I joined

rules.name: Synonym cycling
rules.message: The same thing called three different names in three sentences.
rules.fix: Repeat the clear word, or use a pronoun. Keep a term list (invoice, order, refund) and hold to it.
rules.false_positive_note: Deliberate variation to avoid five repeats in one paragraph.

bad: The agent reviews the draft. The assistant scores the piece. The tool suggests fixes.
good: The agent reviews the draft, scores it, and suggests fixes.

sources: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing (WikiProject AI Cleanup)

rules.name: One metaphor beaten across the piece
rules.message: A single image repeated until it carries nothing.
rules.fix: Use it once, memorably, then let plain language carry the rest.
rules.false_positive_note: A deliberate spine metaphor that does new work each time.

bad: bridges and roads used 30+ times in one article

rules.name: Bullets where prose would read better
rules.message: An argument chopped into bullets.
rules.fix: Write the connected paragraph; keep lists for truly parallel items (and tables for more than four).
rules.false_positive_note: Reference material and steps.

rules.name: Sterile, voiceless prose
rules.message: Clean of tells and also of any person: no opinion, no first person where it is earned, no specific scene.
rules.fix: Add the one thing the author saw that the reader has not: a number, a scene, a plain moral statement.
rules.false_positive_note: Memos and UI copy are meant to be plain.

bad: The experiment produced interesting results. Some developers were impressed while others were skeptical. The implications remain unclear.

rules.name: Overcorrection and manufactured imperfection
rules.message: Slop removal that flattens the piece, or fake mess added to seem human (random typos, forced casualness, profanity the author did not use).
rules.fix: Restore the fact or image that was cut. Mess is never added on purpose.
rules.false_positive_note: Manual check. A real admission, a named mistake or a rough edge that happened is voice, not overcorrection; only invented mess is.

bad: (a rewrite that lost the number to lose the dash)

rules.name: Unsolicited ambient labels and hover text
rules.message: Idle labels or floating text on objects at rest (game objects, tooltips added for flavor).
rules.fix: Placed objects stay silent at rest; flash text only on an action or an error, then clear it. A worn HUD may carry one status line. Run lsl-lint for scripts.
rules.false_positive_note: Transient in-use and error text is fine.

bad: a Home Stone floating the idle label 'Homestone'
a server floating a steady 'Online' label

rules.name: AI-default visual UI tells
rules.message: Purple gradients, Inter everywhere, emoji icon tiles.
rules.fix: Out of scope for this linter; use the impeccable and taste-skill skills.
rules.false_positive_note: Manual check. A gradient, icon tile or card grid that the site's design system already uses on purpose is not a tell.

rules.name: Detector guardrails
rules.message: Linter hits are candidates, and AI detectors are unreliable, with documented bias against non-native writers.
rules.fix: Never use this skill, its score or any detector to claim that a named person used AI.
rules.false_positive_note: Not a pattern. Scoring your own draft for revision is the intended use; only a claim about a named person is out.
sources: Liang et al. 2023, GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers (arXiv:2304.02819)

rules.name: Metaphor asserted as a definition
rules.message: A literal thing is defined as a vivid object ('A newsletter is a conversation that never ends'). The image does the persuading, so the claim never gets its evidence.
rules.fix: Say the literal claim with its number or example, and keep the image only if it survives being stated plainly. If you keep it, it needs to be the only one in the piece.
rules.false_positive_note: Real definitions ('A cache is a store that never expires entries until evicted') match the shape. Read the noun: a literal category is fine, a physical object standing in for a business or idea is the tell. Warn only.

bad: A newsletter is a conversation that never ends.
Your pricing page is a handshake that never ends.
Your calendar is a battlefield where meetings win by default.
Your brand is a promise you make every single day.
good: A cache is a store that returns recent results without recomputing them.
The newsletter goes to 4,000 readers every Tuesday.

rules.name: Reframe pair (they treat X as A. X is B.)
rules.message: Two-sentence reframe: how people see something, then what it really is. It is the X-not-Y device with the negation implied.
rules.fix: Drop the foil sentence and state what the thing is, with the evidence for it.
rules.false_positive_note: A real misconception that the piece goes on to correct with data can stay once per piece. The rule needs the same noun in both sentences.

bad: Teams treat the newsletter as a chore. A newsletter is a conversation that never ends.
Most teams see the audit as a cost. The audit is an insurance policy.
good: Newsletter signups rose from 800 to 1,100 a month once someone owned it.

rules.name: 'That is where the X hides' closer
rules.message: A paragraph-ending stinger that says where the important thing lives ('That gap is where the growth is hiding'). It announces significance and adds no fact.
rules.fix: Cut it, or replace it with the number, name or consequence the paragraph was building to.
rules.false_positive_note: A closing sentence that names a real place or system and carries a figure is fine ('That is where 60 percent of churn happens'); the check ignores sentences that contain a digit.

bad: That gap is where the growth is hiding.
This is where the risk lives.
Pricing is where strategy goes to be tested.
good: That is where 60 percent of churn happens.

rules.name: Paragraph ends on a short line with no fact
rules.message: This paragraph ends on a short sentence, much shorter than the rest, with no number, name or figure in it. It reads as a moral added after the point was made.
rules.fix: Delete the sentence and check that no fact is lost. If one is, fold it into the sentence before.
rules.false_positive_note: A short line that turns the argument is allowed (the density rule short-closer-density counts how many a piece has). Questions, paragraphs under three sentences, cited paragraphs and dialogue are skipped.

bad: The team ran the pilot for six weeks across three offices and measured every referral that came through the new form, then compared the totals against the prior quarter before presenting them to the board. Most of the lift came from one office. The rest was noise.
good: The team ran the pilot for six weeks across three offices and measured every referral that came through the new form. Most of the lift, 22 of 31 referrals, came from the Denver office.

rules.name: Echo stinger
rules.message: The paragraph ends on two short sentences built as a stinger: the second repeats a word and adds a payoff word (nothing, never, more, faster), or flips the first with 'did not'.
rules.fix: Keep the sentence that carries the fact and delete the echo, or join them into one sentence with the evidence.
rules.false_positive_note: Two plain short sentences that each state a fact are fine; the check needs a repeated content word and a payoff word, and skips sentences with a number or a name.

bad: The team built the report. The report built nothing.
Costs fell. Trust fell faster.
The sprint ended. The backlog did not.
good: The team built the report. Finance read it on Monday.

rules.name: Causal glue ('X, enabling Y')
rules.message: A participle clause asserts a consequence ('X, enabling Y') with no evidence that X caused Y or how much.
rules.fix: Say what changed and by how much, or cut the clause. If the effect is real, give the measurement.
rules.false_positive_note: A cause the reader can verify from the sentence itself is fine ('The valve closed, stopping the flow'). Repeated use in one piece is the tell, so a single hit is shown as information only unless the profile sets device_policy to ban.

bad: The team moved the files to one drive, enabling designers to move faster.
We rebuilt the checkout form, helping customers finish in fewer steps.
good: The valve closed and the flow stopped.

rules.name: Unnecessary inference
rules.message: A sentence restates the conclusion the reader already draws from the figure before it ('That means customers were happier').
rules.fix: Delete the sentence, or replace it with a consequence the reader could not infer (a cost, a decision, a date).
rules.false_positive_note: An inference that adds a non-obvious step, such as what the figure implies for next quarter's budget, is fine. Judge it against the preceding sentence.

bad: Complaints fell 42 percent. That means customers were having a better experience.
good: Complaints fell 42 percent. We cut the support team's overtime budget in half.
